review:
Kelvin and the Infamous Machine is a point-and-click adventure game developed and published by Blyts that successfully captures the charm of classic adventure gaming while introducing its own humorous take on time travel and historical mischief. Inspired by the golden era of narrative-driven adventures, the game combines clever puzzle design, colorful visuals, memorable characters, and a lighthearted storyline into an experience that feels both nostalgic and accessible. It embraces the traditions established by genre classics while maintaining enough originality to stand comfortably on its own.

The story follows Kelvin, a young and somewhat inexperienced laboratory assistant who works alongside the brilliant scientist Dr. Edwin Lupin and fellow researcher Lise. What begins as a celebration of a groundbreaking invention quickly turns into chaos when Lupin unveils a functioning time machine and receives ridicule instead of praise from the scientific community. Frustrated and humiliated, he decides to use his invention to travel through history and claim credit for humanity's greatest discoveries and achievements. His actions threaten the integrity of the timeline, forcing Kelvin and Lise to chase him across different eras in an effort to repair the damage before history is permanently altered.

The narrative immediately benefits from its entertaining premise. Time travel has long been a popular theme in adventure games, but Kelvin and the Infamous Machine uses it primarily as a vehicle for comedy. Historical events become playgrounds for absurd situations, allowing players to witness famous figures and moments from entirely new perspectives. The game frequently turns familiar historical concepts upside down, creating humorous scenarios that keep the story engaging from beginning to end.

One of the strongest aspects of the experience is its writing. Dialogue is consistently witty, with characters exchanging humorous observations and playful banter throughout the adventure. The humor relies on clever situations and character interactions rather than constant jokes, allowing the comedy to feel natural. Kelvin serves as an effective protagonist because he is relatable, curious, and often overwhelmed by the increasingly ridiculous circumstances surrounding him. His interactions with both allies and historical figures help maintain the game's cheerful atmosphere.

The time-travel concept provides the foundation for many of the game's most creative puzzles. Rather than simply collecting items and combining objects, players frequently manipulate events across different points in history. Actions performed in one era can have consequences in another, encouraging players to think about cause and effect in inventive ways. This approach gives the puzzle design a unique identity and helps distinguish the game from more traditional point-and-click adventures.

The puzzles generally strike a comfortable balance between challenge and accessibility. Most solutions rely on logic and observation rather than obscure leaps in reasoning. Players are encouraged to experiment with their surroundings, speak to characters, and pay attention to environmental details. While some puzzles require careful thought, the game avoids the frustrating trial-and-error design that occasionally plagued older adventure titles. This makes the experience approachable for newcomers while still providing satisfying moments of discovery.

The historical settings are another major highlight. Throughout the adventure, players visit different time periods and encounter famous individuals whose achievements have been disrupted by Lupin's interference. The game cleverly incorporates these figures into its puzzle structure and narrative progression, allowing players to interact with them in humorous and unexpected ways. These encounters help bring the various eras to life and provide a strong sense of variety as the story unfolds.

Visually, Kelvin and the Infamous Machine embraces a bright and expressive cartoon art style. Every environment is filled with personality, and each historical location possesses its own distinct appearance. Character designs are colorful and exaggerated, complementing the comedic tone of the narrative. The hand-drawn aesthetic gives the game a timeless quality while helping it stand apart from more realistic adventure games.

Character animation contributes significantly to the presentation. Facial expressions, body language, and exaggerated reactions add energy to conversations and comedic moments. Even simple exchanges become more entertaining thanks to the visual personality displayed by the cast. This attention to animation helps maintain engagement during dialogue-heavy sections and reinforces the game's overall charm.

The soundtrack complements the adventure nicely by adapting to the different locations and historical periods. Music helps establish atmosphere without becoming intrusive, supporting both exploration and storytelling. The audio design enhances the sense of travel and discovery while maintaining the playful tone that defines the entire experience.

Another notable strength is the game's pacing. New locations, characters, and puzzle concepts are introduced regularly, ensuring that the adventure never feels stagnant. The narrative moves steadily forward without unnecessary detours, and each chapter contributes something meaningful to the overall story. This structure allows the game to remain entertaining throughout its relatively concise runtime.

The supporting cast further enriches the experience. Lise provides intelligence and determination, helping balance Kelvin's occasional uncertainty, while Dr. Lupin serves as a particularly entertaining antagonist. His motivations stem from wounded pride rather than genuine malice, making him both humorous and surprisingly relatable. The dynamic between the three main characters gives the story a strong emotional core beneath its comedic surface.

Although the game draws clear inspiration from beloved classics such as Day of the Tentacle and other comedic point-and-click adventures, it never feels like a direct imitation. Its emphasis on historical manipulation, original cast, and time-travel-based puzzle solving allows it to establish its own identity. The developers clearly understand what made classic adventure games memorable while also introducing enough fresh ideas to keep the experience feeling modern.

The game's primary weakness is that experienced adventure game veterans may find some puzzles relatively straightforward. The overall challenge level is moderate, and the story can be completed without becoming excessively demanding. However, this accessibility is also one of the reasons the game appeals to a broader audience. Players unfamiliar with the genre can enjoy the adventure without becoming overwhelmed by overly complicated puzzle chains.

Kelvin and the Infamous Machine ultimately succeeds as a delightful adventure filled with humor, creativity, and charm. Its engaging story, intelligent puzzle design, memorable characters, and imaginative use of time travel combine to create an experience that remains entertaining throughout its entire journey. While it may not revolutionize the genre, it demonstrates a deep appreciation for classic adventure design and delivers a polished experience that fans of narrative-driven games are likely to appreciate.

The puzzles are fair, and the story is a fun little journey to meet irl geniuses in a fictional setting and you as the protagonist gives them the nudge they need to overcome "writers block" so to speak on their groundbreaking invention, but get caught up in having to go through silly antics and hoops to do so (the puzzles). Overall for the price tag I'd say it's worth it. I actually wish they made it twice as long and charged like 19.99 or something because I was enjoying it and was sad for the game to end.

A funny game with good voice acting, with mostly serviceable gameplay. 
I played only the first chapter but it can be summed up as typical [i]point & click[/i] series of actions focused on obtaining a certain outcome by finding items, exchanging item, combining items, etc. 

So far so good.

[b]HOWEVER[/b]...
I have to give it up for developer Blyts for finding a way to make even the dreaded [i]moon logic[/i] look good in comparison to the logic-devoid nonsense they pulled off at the end of the first chapter of this game, which lead me to immediately get a refund.
[spoiler]Your mission is to make Beethoven write his Fifth Symphony. The only 'puzzles' left in the chapter are a group of drunks wanting to toast with you with a tankard, a rock-paper-scissors competition with a mysterious extra rule that rewards a tankard, a fortuneteller that can help you figure out where to find the game's rules if she has playing/tarot cards, and finally a man with playing cards who can be tricked into drinking a cocktail (that you have!) that will knock him out.
You can see the obvious path from A to B, B to C, C to D and D to E. But how does E get you to X (Beethoven writing his symphony)? Excellent question! The developer clearly had no idea either, so... IT JUST DOES! Isn't that hilaaaaaaaarious?!
Sigh.[/spoiler]

Lamentablemente tengo que bajarle el pulgar a esta aventura gráfica. No me voy a extender demasiado como suelo hacer en otras reseñas, simplemente decir que tiene varios aspectos positivos, empezando por su estética, el arte del juego es un lujo, digno de las mejores aventuras gráficas. Los sonidos y las voces también son de muy buena calidad... en síntesis, podríamos decir que el juego es muy bueno técnicamente hablando. La historia, parte de una idea ingeniosa... entonces [b] ¿por qué la calificación negativa? [/b] Bueno, es simple, el juego falla en lo más importante: divertir, entretener, y sobre todo en la manera en que se desarrolla. En una aventura gráfica de tan corta duración (menos de cuatro horas de juego) los puzzles son todo. Si los puzzles y la manera en que se desarrolla la historia falla, entonces falla todo, no importa que tan original sea la premisa. En ese sentido, el juego falla terriblemente.

Es muy dificil (por no decir imposible) resolver algunos puzzles, dado que carecen absolutamente de lógica. Además, carecen de contexto o propósito. Si te dijeran que tenés que lograr "tal cosa", pensarías de qué manera podrías realizarla, pero si no te dicen cuál es esa cosa u objetivo, simplemente te tiran en una locación (con la excusa de la máquina del tiempo) y te dejan ahí tirado, ¿qué haces? La única manera de avanzar es probando todo lo que vas encontrando por el escenario. Trama ingeniosa pero la manera de hacer que se desarrolle es super pobre y forzada. Lamento darle negativo porque se ve que es un juego realizado (técnica y artísticamente) con mucho cuidado, pero sinceramente no podría recomendarlo a un conocido o amigo, ya que es un bodrio como solemos decir por estos pagos, aburridísimo a más no poder, a pesar de sus intentos de ser gracioso en algunos diálogos y conversaciones.

TLDR: An incredibly simple adventure that doesn’t take anything seriously. 

[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]

Kelvin and the infamous machine (KIM) is an over the top, light hearted, Saturday morning cartoon feeling kind of point and click adventure. Our villain is a mad scientist on route to destroy the universe with time travel, and our plucky muppet must bumble his way through three time periods to help famous figures complete their most famous works and right the timeline. 

Kelvin himself is the archetypal ‘idiot protagonist’. He feels like someone put Gary Goodspeed from Final Space into a point and click adventure. The puzzles are mostly straight forward fare for PnC vets. Grab a random assortment of junk, rub said junk on anything with a name, and talk to everyone over and over. While there is a bit of moon logic, mostly pretend you’re in the Saturday morning cartoon and you’ll be fine. 

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Wonderfully simple art, music, and sound effects. It’s quite easy to get absorbed into and play KIM thanks to the design being quite stripped back.
[*] The voice acting is delightful, and it feels like everyone, including side characters, are both into and enjoying their roles. 
[*] KIM gave me a few laugh out loud moments. I’d be hesitant to call it ‘funny’, per say, but if you embrace the silly and let it, it’ll give you some childish giggles. 
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The aiming of this feels a bit off. The art, sound, acting, etc. would suggest the game is aimed at kids. But the puzzles, while mostly logical, can be extremely frustrating at points. They require quite a few steps and a lot of sideways knowledge and lateral thinking to fully pull off.  
[*] The lack of a skip cutscene button and some unskippable dialogue make various sections tedious. The long transitions between scenes doesn’t help this, with Kelvin ambling across the screen like he’s got all day. 
[*] KIM doesn’t do anything new. This isn’t a story one will remember, in exactly the same way as 90% of those cartoons never stuck. The characters will sort of merge into one, the puzzles are so meh level that they won’t stick, the story draws so heavily on other media that you’ll just forget it, and it gives it this overall disposable feeling. 
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
 [list][*] Skip cutscene button, and make all dialogue skippable. 
[*] Hotspot highlight should also show exits.
[*] A double click to move, or skip animation button, so I can zoooooom around.
[*] I’d have liked a slot based save system so my achievement run could’ve been done in 10 minutes instead of a little over an hour. 
[/list]


[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]

DO NOT BUY THIS IF IT IS NOT ON SALE.

Seriously. This is a two quid game not a ten quid game, and it goes on sale for exactly that.

That said, I give this a solid thumbs up as a game. It’s frustrating until you solve it, as a puzzler should be. It’s got that self-referential and irreverent humour that made the original point and clicks the absolute icons that they are. It’s smooth and easy to play, with good enough everything. All round this is a solid addition to anyone looking for something casual. It’s also super short. It took me around two and a half hours with no guide, with another hour to 100% 

As such, this is not for a point and click vet looking for a challenge. It isn’t for someone looking for some whizzbang and a bunch of explosions, it isn’t for someone looking for a meaningful story experience, and it isn’t for someone looking for something serious.

KIM is a Saturday morning cartoon in point and click form, and if you're embracing and accepting of that, I think you’ll have a good time.
